title: Maximal chains of primes in a Cohen–Macaulay local ring have length the dimension
statement: Let $(S,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] of Krull dimension $d=\dim S$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring] (finite, as $S$ is Noetherian local), and assume that $S$ is Cohen–Macaulay in the sense that $\operatorname{depth}(S)\ge d$ [def-weil-pbc-depth], that is, $\mathfrak m$ contains an $S$-regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence] of length $d$. Let $\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_n$ be a maximal chain of prime ideals of $S$, that is, a chain of prime ideals that cannot be lengthened by inserting a prime ideal before $\mathfrak p_0$, between two consecutive members, or after $\mathfrak p_n$ (so $\mathfrak p_0$ is a minimal prime ideal of $S$, $\mathfrak p_n=\mathfrak m$, and no prime ideal lies strictly between $\mathfrak p_{i-1}$ and $\mathfrak p_i$). Then $n=d$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00N9 (lemma-maximal-chain-CM, line 25345: 'Let R be Noetherian local. Suppose R is Cohen-Macaulay of dimension d. Any maximal chain of ideals p_0 ⊂ p_1 ⊂ ... ⊂ p_n has length n = d'), proved there as a special case of lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-CM (line 25151); Cohen-Macaulay local ring as in definition-local-ring-CM (line 25308)

proof.text: (Induction set-up.) We prove by induction on the integer $d\ge0$ the claim $P(d)$: for every Noetherian local ring $(S,\mathfrak m)$ with $\dim S=d$ and $\operatorname{depth}(S)\ge d$, every maximal chain $\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_n$ of prime ideals of $S$ has $n=d$. Two remarks on such a chain. (i) $n\le d$, since $\dim S$ is the supremum of the lengths of chains of primes [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. (ii) $\mathfrak p_n=\mathfrak m$ (every prime of the local ring $S$ lies in $\mathfrak m$, so $\mathfrak m$ could otherwise be appended) and $\mathfrak p_0$ is a minimal prime of $S$ (otherwise a smaller prime could be prepended); and no prime lies strictly between $\mathfrak p_{i-1}$ and $\mathfrak p_i$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0AAE (lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-CM, line 25151), proof, for M = R, 'We will prove this by induction on dim(R)'

proof.text: (Base $d=0$.) By remark (i) of Step 1, $0\le n\le d=0$, so $n=0=d$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0AAE (lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-CM, line 25151), proof, for M = R, 'If dim(R) = 0, then the statement is clear'

proof.text: (For $d>0$ we have $n\ge1$.) Suppose $d>0$ and $n=0$. Then $\mathfrak p_0=\mathfrak m$ by Step 1 (ii), and $\mathfrak m$ is a minimal prime. Every prime $\mathfrak q$ of $S$ satisfies $\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak m$, hence $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak m$ by minimality; so $S$ has exactly one prime ideal and every chain of primes has length $0$, i.e. $\dim S=0$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring], a contradiction. Hence $n\ge1$ and $\mathfrak p_1$ exists.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0AAE (lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-CM, line 25151), proof, for M = R, 'Assume dim(R) > 0. Then n > 0'

proof.text:
(Choice of $x$.) Let $d>0$ and assume $P(d-1)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finitely-many-minimal-primes] $S$ has finitely many minimal primes $\mathfrak q_1,\dots,\mathfrak q_r$ ($r\ge1$; $\mathfrak p_0$ is one of them). For each $j$, $\mathfrak p_1
ot\subseteq\mathfrak q_j$: otherwise $\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subseteq\mathfrak q_j$ exhibits a prime strictly inside the minimal prime $\mathfrak q_j$. Prime avoidance [lem-weil-pbc-prime-avoidance], with $J=\mathfrak p_1$ and the prime ideals $I_j=\mathfrak q_j$, gives $x\in\mathfrak p_1$ with $x
otin\mathfrak q_j$ for all $j$. In particular $x\in\mathfrak p_1\subseteq\mathfrak m$ and $x
otin\mathfrak p_0$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0AAE (lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-CM, line 25151), proof, for M = R, 'Choose an element x in p_1, with x not in any of the minimal primes of R ... (See Lemma 00DS)'

proof.text: ($\mathfrak p_1$ is associated to $S/x^kS$.) By [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-minimal-prime-associated] the minimal prime $\mathfrak p_0$ is an associated prime of $S$: $\mathfrak p_0=\operatorname{Ann}_S(z)$ for some $z\in S$. The prime $\mathfrak p_1$ is minimal over $\mathfrak p_0+(x)$: it contains $\mathfrak p_0$ and $x$; and if $\mathfrak q$ is a prime with $\mathfrak p_0+(x)\subseteq\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak p_1$, then $\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak q$ because $x\in\mathfrak q\setminus\mathfrak p_0$ (Step 4), so $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak p_1$ since no prime lies strictly between $\mathfrak p_0$ and $\mathfrak p_1$ (Step 1 (ii)). Apply [lem-weil-pbc-associated-prime-power-quotient] to the local ring $S$, the finite $S$-module $M=S$ (generated by $1$), $x\in\mathfrak m$, $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_0$ and $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak p_1$: there are $k\ge1$ and $w\in S/x^kS$ with $\operatorname{Ann}_S(w)=\mathfrak p_1$. Put $y=x^k$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0AAE (lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-CM, line 25151), proof, for M = R, 'After replacing x by x^n for some n, we may assume that p_1 is an associated prime of M/xM, see Lemma 0CN5'; the hypothesis p_0 in Ass(R) from Lemma Tag 05BV (lemma-ass-minimal-prime-support)

proof.text: ($S/yS$ is a Cohen–Macaulay local ring of dimension $d-1$.) We have $y=x^k\in\mathfrak p_1\subseteq\mathfrak m$, and $y$ lies in no minimal prime $\mathfrak q_j$, since $x\notin\mathfrak q_j$ and $\mathfrak q_j$ is prime. By [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-local-dim-drop-outside-minimal-primes], $\dim(S/yS)=d-1$. Hence [lem-weil-pbc-cm-local-dimension-drop-regular-sequence], applied with $c=1$ and $g_1=y$ (its hypotheses: $S$ Noetherian local, $\dim S=d$ finite, $\operatorname{depth}(S)\ge d$, $\dim S/(y)=d-1$), shows that $y$ is an $S$-regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence], in particular a nonzerodivisor on $S$. Then [lem-weil-pbc-cm-local-quotient-nonzerodivisor-cm] gives that $T:=S/yS$ is a Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m/yS$, $\dim T=d-1$, and $\operatorname{depth}(T)\ge d-1$ [def-weil-pbc-depth].

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0AAE (lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-CM, line 25151), proof, for M = R, 'Then dim(R/xR) = dim(R) - 1 by Lemma 00KW. The module M/xM is Cohen-Macaulay over R/xR by Proposition 00N6 and Lemma 0AAD'; the module form 0B52 (lemma-one-equation-module) and Lemma Tag 02JN (lemma-reformulate-CM) for M = R

proof.text: ($\mathfrak p_1/yS$ is a minimal prime of $T$.) Since $y\in\mathfrak p_1$, $\bar{\mathfrak p}_1:=\mathfrak p_1/yS$ is a prime ideal of $T$. The $S$-module structure of $S/yS$ is the restriction of its $T$-module structure along $S\to T$, so for $a\in S$ with image $\bar a\in T$ we have $\bar a w=aw$; hence $\operatorname{Ann}_T(w)=\{\bar a: a\in\operatorname{Ann}_S(w)\}=\mathfrak p_1/yS$ (Step 5). Thus $\bar{\mathfrak p}_1$ is an associated prime of $T$, and $T$ is a Noetherian local ring with $\operatorname{depth}(T)\ge\dim T=d-1$ (Step 6). By [lem-weil-pbc-cm-local-associated-prime-minimal] applied to $T$, $\bar{\mathfrak p}_1$ is a minimal prime ideal of $T$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0AAE (lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-CM, line 25151), proof, for M = R, 'By Lemma 0BUS we conclude that p_1/(x) is a minimal prime of R/xR'; the support statement (Lemma Tag 00L3, lemma-support-quotient) is not needed for M = R

proof.text: (Conclusion.) The prime ideals of $T=S/yS$ are the $\mathfrak Q/yS$ with $\mathfrak Q$ a prime of $S$ containing $y$, with inclusions preserved and reflected. As $y\in\mathfrak p_1\subseteq\mathfrak p_i$ for $i\ge1$, $\mathfrak p_1/yS\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_n/yS$ is a chain of primes of $T$ of length $n-1$. It is a maximal chain: nothing can be inserted before $\mathfrak p_1/yS$ (minimal by Step 7); a prime $\mathfrak Q/yS$ strictly between $\mathfrak p_{i-1}/yS$ and $\mathfrak p_i/yS$ would give a prime $\mathfrak Q$ of $S$ strictly between $\mathfrak p_{i-1}$ and $\mathfrak p_i$, impossible (Step 1 (ii)); and $\mathfrak p_n/yS=\mathfrak m/yS$ is the maximal ideal of the local ring $T$. By the induction hypothesis $P(d-1)$ applied to $T$ (Noetherian local, $\dim T=d-1$, $\operatorname{depth}(T)\ge d-1$, Step 6), $n-1=d-1$, so $n=d$. This proves $P(d)$, hence the statement.
